utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please bring in the accused. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I hope that everyone can hear me. Are the interpreters here? Now can the Defence hear me all right, and the Prosecution? All right, as we agreed, we are going to try to work in the spirit of serenity today. Mr. Kehoe, you now have the floor. I understand that you have the very heavy responsibility today to do what you can to try to end this examination within the time period we have allotted. I talked about working in serenity. Both parties will be controlling the clock today, otherwise we will be required to bring the witness back, so counsel, Mr. Kehoe, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will move briefly through my initial remarks, consistent with the court's plan. I will say that there will be very few questions by the Prosecutor during this examination. It will be in the narrative for, I would say, over 90 per cent of his testimony. The testimony focuses, your Honours, on, in large part, the allegations set forth in 5.2 of the indictment. As you know, it is part of charging crimes against humanity, the Prosecutor must prove that the actions were widespread and systematic and large scale. Our particular indictment charges widespread, large scale and systematic persecution of the Bosnian Muslim population, not only in those townships, in those municipalities under the command of the defendant Blaskic, Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak but this occurred as part of a larger plan throughout what we have heard so much about, called Herceg-Bosna. The next witness is a reporter for The Guardian who has received many commendations from the international community as well as being the author of a book known as "Seasons in Hell". He will explain to you his travels and his experiences through Central and southern Bosnia, specifically Herzegovina, and how he determined there was a plan, a plan from the top coming from Mate Boban, the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and working its way to the HVO troops on the command, including the troops commanded by the defendant, Blaskic. He will describe what he saw after his conversations with Mate Boban in August and October of 1992 and how he then observed, based -- after those conversations, how the ethnic cleansing commenced and the ethnic cleansing commenced of the Muslim population by the HVO. You will hear several municipalities, I do not believe, your Honours, that you have heard of before, they are nevertheless listed in paragraph 5.2 on the widespread and systematic count. They are and will be commented on by the witness, Duvno, which has also been described by the name Tomislavgrad. Tomislavgrad is the same municipality as Duvno. In the indictment we have it listed as Duvno. Another municipality, Stolac. Your Honours have heard of Mostar, there will be discussion about the ethnic cleansing in Prozor and in Capljina. What the witness will describe to you, based on his experience in the former Yugoslavia and in the conflict in Bosnia, that the activities on the HVO were systematic, they were organised, there was direction, it came from the top and went to the bottom and there was a plan, an overall plan, to ethnically cleanse the Muslim and certainly marginalise the Muslims from what had been described as Herceg-Bosna. In the interests of time, I do not think it is necessary to go into all those facts that the witness will talk about, suffice it to say that he will, in large part, give your Honours the explanation about how what happened in Vitez -- in Vitez and Kiseljak and Busovaca under the command of the defendant was something that was part of a much larger fabric, that was happening throughout various areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, let us bring in the witness now. He is a journalist from The Guardian, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, The Guardian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please state your name and your first name, in that order. First your last name, then your first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vulliamy Edward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing so you may read the solemn declaration which will be your oath. MR. EDWARD VULLIAMY (Sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may be seated. You have been asked to appear here before the International Criminal Tribunal in this trial against Mr. Blaskic, the person who is here in this courtroom. It is the Prosecutor who has called for you to appear. He is the one who will begin by asking you questions. He has given us a brief summary about your testimony and he has given us an idea also what will be included in your testimony. Now, perhaps we will give the floor to the Prosecution, so he can introduce his first remarks and questions. Examined by MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just preliminary questions before we go into the substance of your testimony. Could you tell the judges a little about yourself, what you do for a living, how long you have done it, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I have been a , journalist since 1977. I was a television reporter from 1978 until 1986, when I joined the daily newspaper, The Guardian of London, by whom I have been employed ever since. I have developed to the level of what I think is called "international reporter", which means you work all over the place, and by default have become a war reporter, without intending to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us a little more, Mr. Vulliamy, you became an international reporter. Tell us where you have been stationed and what you have covered, specifically over the past decade or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I made films all over the place; Middle East, Lebanon, Europe, United States. For The Guardian, since I went on the road, as were, I covered the fall of Communism in eastern Europe, Germany, Romania. I worked in Northern Ireland, I covered the Gulf War from Iraq until -- up until the war and just after it. And, in 1990, I was based in Italy on a brief that was to cover Italy and I may occasionally have to go to Yugoslavia, they said. The reality, for obvious reasons, turned out to be the other way round. I was in Slovenia and Croatia during the wars there -- the conflict in Slovenia and the war of independence in Croatia, working in Vukovar, Vinkovci, Osejak and all over Croatia. Then in 1992, subject to my brief, followed the violence down into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you covered the activities in the former Yugoslavia, Croatia and Bosnia from 1991 through approximately 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on and off I was there from the beginning to the end, with a year off between 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your writing in the international field, have you been the recipient of various awards from international organisations, as well as other press organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes, I have won -- if you might want to know, I won International Reporter of the Year, 1992, a thing called Correspondent of the Year in 1992, Amnesty International Reporter of the Year, 1992, the James Cameron Award, which, rightly or wrongly, is called the "British Pulitzer", in 1994, then International Reporter of the Year 1996 for a retrospective series I wrote about the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us turn our attention to the events in the former Yugoslavia. Could you tell the judges briefly your entry into the events in Yugoslavia and then focus the large part of your narrative on the events taking place between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats over the 93/94 period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. As I said, I had covered the war in Croatia for its duration from July -- June/July 1991 through to the conclusion at the end of the year. My work in Bosnia began -- focused almost entirely upon violence being inflicted by the Serbs against the Croatian and Muslim populations. I was the person who, with the film crew, uncovered the Serb camps at Omarska and Trnopolje. In August 1992 I was working also in Sarajevo. I was quite well attuned to the war by the time I came upon the possibility of conflict between the Croatians and the Government army. It was -- there were strange reports around and I was aware of them before I first met Mr. Boban. First of all, a meeting in a Vojvodina area of Yugoslavia in 1991 between President Tudjman of Croatia and President Milosevic of Serbia. We knew there were rumours that there had been some sort of carve up of Bosnia discussed at that meeting, that had been reported. It was around, it was in the back of our minds. As were reports, odd though they seemed at the time, of a meeting in Graz, which had also been covered and was public, between Mr. Mate Boban, who was the President of Herceg-Bosna, a statelet within Bosnia declared in March 1992, before Bosnia was even independent of Yugoslavia. One was vaguely aware of these things but they were very much in the back of one's mind, because of what was happening on the ground which seemed to be at odds with all this. Serbs were meting out some particularly savage violence against both the Muslims and the Croats, and they seemed to be resisting as allies to this. I first met Mr. Boban in August 1992, August 13th. This was after -- I was actually responding to a challenge from the Serbs after we found their camps. They said: “Well, go and look at the camps which are being run for our people by the Croats". I thought, fair enough, I will. It is my job. So I did and I investigated a camp which I will not trouble you with now, Serb prisoners, and discussed, went to discuss this with Mr. Boban. There was an internecine conflict going on between Mr. Boban's HVO and a small militia called the HOS which was around at that time. We went to see him. We discussed both of these things a bit, but he wanted to talk about other things too. He was the President of Herceg-Bosna, the statelet but not of the Party, the HDZ, which was the Bosnian branch of President Tudjman's ruling Party in Croatia. He talked a lot about Herceg-Bosna that night. It was in his office in Grude off the main street, little town of Grude, which was his administrative capital from which he ran Herceg-Bosna, because the fighting was too heavy in Mostar, which he claimed was the capital of Herceg-Bosna. He said it was: "Spiritually, culturally and economically part of Croatia", from which it had been separated by what he called: "Unfortunate historical circumstances". Given the nature of the war, I took historical circumstances to mean deep history, centuries. I now realise what he meant was the independence of Croatia from Yugoslavia and the fact that Bosnia had only just become independent. He said he could not accept the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its capital, Sarajevo, because he said that constitution, although it defended individual rights, it did not defend the rights of people, the word is "Narod" which I had come to know to mean "people and nation", or "race", at the same time. Those were the rights that he was interested in protecting. He did not think the constitution guaranteed the rights of his people, the Croatian people, the Narod. He went on to say -- he thought -- he called Bosnia-Herzegovina: "Historically Croatian living space". Those are the rather unfortunate terms the translator used, I kept it. Went on to argue for a dismemberment of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of what he called "cantons" or "provinces". He said then that this was based on an idea inspired by Switzerland and was the spirit of the European Union. I take it he meant at the time he wanted this to appeal to western ears. With hindsight, if you will allow me, this language of "cantons" and "provinces" would later echo that of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Dr. Owen had not been appointed yet into the peace process and would not for a couple of weeks. The plan would not be published for several months. With hindsight, this echo was there. His last point was that this time, he said, the Croatian people are armed and equipped to defend their freedom. We drove away from this conversation, said our goodbyes and talked about it in some detail, because it was an interesting conversation. The first thing that struck me about this was that the gist of the briefing -- and it was a long conversation, it lasted at least two hours -- was directed much more against his supposed Muslim allies and the Government in Sarajevo to which he was, I thought, loyal, until this conversation, than it was against his supposed Serb enemy. I began to sort of remember this vaguely from the back of my mind, this talk about a deal in the Vojvodina between Presidents Tudjman and Milosevic and this bizarre report of a meeting between himself and Dr. Karadzic, the leader of the Bosnian Serbs in Graz earlier that year. My colleague did actually ask Mr. Boban had he ever met Karadzic and he said no, he had not. The gist of this was against Sarajevo and his allies, which is all the more peculiar because a matter of a couple of weeks beforehand, the mainly Muslim -- although not entirely then -- Muslim Bosnian Army had fought alongside the HVO in one of the more remarkable military successes of their alliance, when they had driven the Serbs out of the eastern half of Mostar, east of the Neretva River, and up a mountain into the hills. It was quite an achievement and the atmosphere in Mostar -- I has also been on that trip -- was still in the aura of this victory. Boban's remarks seemed peculiar in the light of that. The second thing was that he clearly saw Herceg-Bosna as no part of Bosnia-Herzegovina but part of Croatia, for all his caveats. There was this use of the term: "We are armed and equipped to defend our freedom." We were, rather sadly, accustomed to this kind of language, meaning: "We are prepared to impose our will by freedom in the former Yugoslavia", by this time. Anyway, that conversation got lost in other work. The priorities of the day were what the Serbs were doing to Croats and Muslims in the country elsewhere. I carried on working with that. Bumped into this theme again into September 1992, when I went up to Travnik. I had accompanied some Muslims and Croats over the mountains when they were being herded over the hills from their homes by the Serbs at the end of August and had been dumped in this town, Travnik in Central Bosnia. I wanted to go back and report on that. I heard strange reports of a shooting incident in a place called Kiseljak between Muslims and Croats. It seemed odd. And another shoot-out, isolated incident, at an arms factory in Novi Travnik which was another town, separate from Travnik, just a little way up the valley. I did not know anything about these. I was hearing from -- about them from one young man in particular who found it all abhorrent. He was the commander of the HVO in Travnik, I knew him from the first war in Croatia, a man called Pokrajcic. He said that he was not going to bow, as he put it, to pressure from either side, implying there was pressure from the Muslim and Croat side -- he did not explain what, but he said, and I quote, or something like it: "Over my dead body will I submit to this pressure, I am here to fight for the two victim peoples of this war". I took that, rightly, to mean the Croats and the Muslims. Something was in the air. As I say, the Serbs were still the priority. I let that go. I move on to October of that year, the following month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, yes, sorry. There was an interesting -- we were watching the pattern of fighting obviously very careful. There was some interesting developments. It seemed that there were very few -- there was very little fighting going on between the HVO, south of Central Bosnia anyway, and the Serbs, that the Croatians were moving their troops into areas which were Muslim-controlled, in which there were more Croats than Serbs and that the Serbs, meanwhile, were focusing their attention on areas which were Muslim-controlled in which there were more Serbs than Croats; Srebrenica, Korasde, I do not need to go into that, it is a tangent. Because of this development, the idea of the carve up came back into one's mind again and then things started to happen very rapidly and suddenly. I was in Split, where we were often based for logistical reasons, on the Croatian coast, when I heard, and this was on October 20, 1992, that Mate Boban had been up to Travnik and had declared it part of Herceg-Bosna. Well, this was quite a shock and quite important because Travnik was a very long way up the line into Central Bosnia. It was a matter of a few miles from the Serb -- the front-line with the Serbs. It was way up into Central Bosnia. It had a Muslim -- the Muslims where by quite a way, I think, the largest ethnic group in the town, and it was a surprise that Boban had gone up there and declared this as part of the Herceg-Bosna, particularly when I recalled what Herceg-Bosna was supposed to be, according to his briefing of August 15th, the bellicose position that Herceg-Bosna was taking with regards to the Sarajevo government. I was surprised. Things moved very, very fast. The next day, October 21st, reports reached us of a shoot-out of a gas station in Novi Travnik. The reason for it apparently -- and I add hindsight here, because I did not find this out until later -- was that supplies were being equally divided up until then in Central Bosnia between the Bosnian Army, mainly Muslim and the HVO. Apparently -- so the story goes -- the HVO said to the Muslim guy going to get the fuel: "sorry, you are not getting your share". There had been an argument and somebody shot the Muslim soldier dead. We were trying to guess whether this was just an isolated accident or something serious. Given what Boban said, what he had been saying in Travnik the day before, we decided to go up and have a look. What we found was surprising and depressing. We took a route up through Mostar and Kiseljak, through Busovaca and there was a lot of movement on the road, particularly from Kiseljak, a lot of trucks and ramshackle vehicles carrying soldiers into the Vitez, Novi Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO, all HVO. Sorry, unless I say otherwise, Croatian will mean HVO. It got dark, we failed to reach Novi Travnik before dark and did not want to because the atmosphere had completely changed. There were road blocks along most of the way, new road blocks, HVO road blocks. We got as far as Vitez and went -- we were killing time and went to a radio forum in a house where a radio station was quartered. There all the parties to this, shall we say, embryonic conflict, were represented; the local imam, the Croatian HDZ and the HVO. The HVO was represented by a man called Pero Skopljak. I remember him and took a note of him saying that: "The HVO was now the only legal authority", in the area where power had been previously shared. There was -- that was the first time I heard of the village of Ahmici -- pure coincidence, I was going through my notes later. There was a reference to Ahmici, the man from the HDZ, I do not know his name, said that Ahmici, the Muslims had been singing songs which offended the Croats. I would ask you to understand that had we known what else was going to happen, we would have taken more notes, but the forum was dull for the most part, and I did not take any more. I just saw that name, but they were talking about something that happened in Ahmici and the Croats were taking exception to it. The reason I did not take any notes of the debate is because of what was happening outside. The building had a balcony overlooking the part of the town and there was a lot of fighting going on. People came out to explain, they said that the Muslims had put barricades up in Stari Vitez, which means "old Vitez", their quarter, and were shooting out. That, I am sure they were. We could see a lot of shooting in from positions that were visible from the balcony. I did not see, but I could hear, because I knew the sound of it by now, anti-aircraft weapons being launched, ground-to-ground. There was a lot of fighting. The meeting broke up and we were quite wary of what to do and where to go. We decided to go and stay, as we had done before -- when I say "we" in this instance it is a chap called Sasha (Inaudible), a good guy, a Croatian -- quite a hard-line Croatian, actually. We decided to go to the Hotel Vitez. The system roughly is this: the HVO had two hotels in the area, the Orient in Travnik and the Hotel Vitez in Vitez. The system was roughly this, they were militarised, they were billeting soldiers there. If you rolled up and offered some Deutschmarks to stay the night, they were only too happy to move a soldier to another room, everybody was happy, you got a place to sleep, that was fine. We said: "Let's stay at the Hotel Vitez". We arrived there to find the place completely transformed since our last visit there. There were men bunkering down in the lobby, men bunkering down in the bar. We were told we could not stay, that it was now a military headquarters. Actually Sasha knew one of the guys and said: "Look, this is silly, it is dark, we do not want to go out, there are road blocks, there is shooting; can we stay and we will pay as usual?"; "No, sorry, orders. Cannot do it, love to help you, you have got to go". Not pleasant. We left that night out into -- through the road blocks, picked up a Muslim man whose car had been hijacked, dropped him off somewhere, menacing atmosphere, found somewhere to sleep. Hotel Vitez obviously out of action, closed to the public from now on. Next day got up -- we found a bed in Fojnica, got up, drove back to Novi Travnik, aiming to get into the centre of the town to see what fighting was going on. Could not get to the centre of the town, got trapped behind a wall. The Croat -- we were with the HVO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sorry, which day was that? What day exactly, you stated that earlier but I did not hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that I did, actually. October 22nd was the day we drove up and stayed where -- where the radio debate took place, in the hotel. The next day is the 23rd, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Even though our time is being counted, could you please speak a little more slowly for the interpreters, because you are speaking too quickly and it is difficult for them to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies to you and the interpreters. Next day, October 23rd, we got up, go up heading for Novi Travnik. Cannot get there because of the fighting. We end up being pinned behind a wall with some HVO soldiers. They are from, they said, Vitez and Tomislavgrad, otherwise known as Duvno, its previous name. They were firing these anti-aircraft guns, ground-to-ground, shoulder-launched. They are powerful. We were pinned behind the wall by a Muslim sniper who was shooting anyone who tried to run back to the car. We stayed there for some hours. It was quite scary because the person I was with told me she was a haemophilic, which was not exactly reassuring. So eventually we got out and went to a hospital in Travnik. I knew the director of the hospital quite well by this time. He had spent the war hitherto treating Muslims and Croats alike, who had been ripped apart by sniper and mortar fire from the Serbs; now he was treating Muslims and Croats alike who had been ripped apart by each other. The interviews we did in there that day included two young children, one of each, as it so happened. Well, we left Novi Travnik that night to return down to the telephones. Pretty bewildered; here was an all-out war going on now, only -- we are now only 48 hours after Boban's visit to Travnik. This was a war for the first time in all my time in Yugoslavia in which the Serbs were not involved. We joked about them laughing about it on top of the mountains. They could see the whole thing, I presume. Got back to Split to find from colleagues that we needed to get on the road again quickly because an ultimatum had been issued in Mostar, which was the capital of Herceg-Bosna, or aspirant capital, by the HVO to the Bosnian Army that it was to disarm immediately and either to disband or come under HVO control. We did not know what to expect, went up to Mostar early next morning. In Mostar, the situation had changed completely from the alliance of the summer. The HVO had taken over the court house, the city hall, the post office, the telecommunications building, they had put a guard outside the headquarters of the Bosnian Army which then was next door in the western half of the city, the less exposed half -- exposed to the Serbs, that is. We went in to interview the commander, a man called Arif Pasalic, who told us --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander of which side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Army, we went through the Croatian guard to get into the Bosnian headquarters to interview their commander. Sorry, Pasalic, his name. He said he had been told to disarm. He said: "I refuse to disarm, how can I disarm during a war?", was what he said. He also said: "This is not some local squabble. This is the implementation of a plan, a policy coming from Grude and Mate Boban. If it is implemented here it will mean war in Mostar", which I took -- as it turned out, rightly -- to mean not war in Mostar as there had been over the past few months but war within Mostar between the two erstwhile allies. We went around the town to find that the HVO had done something else. They had taken all the Muslim refugees out of their places of refuge and insisted they go to HVO headquarters to get new papers issued by the HVO and stamped by the HVO, if they wished to continue to remain sheltered in Mostar. These were mostly Muslims from areas now under Serb control. We completed our visit by going to see the HVO commander at his headquarters which was, and I remember this, bristling with new weapons. You go into the barracks and there is a few guns lying around and everybody has a gun. There was a lot of boxes of ammunition being piled up, new sand-bagging around the walls. We sat down with the commander, Lasic, who poured us some rather good scotch, as I recall, and explained to us that the HVO was now -- and I took a note of this, I thought it interesting -- "The sole civilian military authority in the town, in the city". I was interested in this entwinement of the terms "civilian" and "military". It was also that remark was interesting because it echoed almost exactly what Mr. Skopljak had said back in Vitez, a long way away. Commander Lasic then said that there would be again: "No legal Muslim representation in Mostar" from thereon in. Then we asked him: "What about the army?" He said: "The army should disarm and I am inviting them to remove themselves from the front-lines". This was particularly ironic. He was arguing that the HVO would be better off defending Mostar from the Serbs if the Bosnian Army were to be removed from the front-lines. We knew that the Bosnian Army positions to the east of Mostar were quite a long way forward from those of the HVO, so it was military nonsense that they would be stronger for withdrawing them, because the front-line would come back towards the city, if the Serbs cared to take up the opportunity. Again, so in the back of one's mind, the spectre of this carve up re-emerges because the border between what was supposed to be the Muslim -- the deal between the Serbs and the Croats was that -- was meant to be Mostar. Anyway, in conclusion, we left Mostar disheartened by all this, disheartened by the similarity of the rhetoric, this was happening -- it was coherent, same thing was happening in Mostar, Vitez, Novi Travnik and we did not know where else. The timeframe was alarming in its speed. We were only still two or three days away from Mr. Boban's visit to Travnik, from the first shot at a gas station had suddenly become this. By its apparent coherence. I think we sort of tried to pretend it was not happening, frankly, but we now had a war between the people who had been allies. Anyway, we were heading back to Split and thought: "Hang on, there is a conversation we need to have about all this, and it is with Mate Boban", so we -- we decided to reroute through Grude, although it is getting late, and to find Mate Boban again. We went to Grude --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a date on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24th October, a Saturday, as I recall. October 24th. We go to see Mate Boban again. "We" this time is myself and a guy from Reuters. We went to Grude, he had moved headquarters, he moved to an expanded seat, he was now in a hotel across the road from his old office. I think it was called Hotel Grude, but I am not absolutely certain of that. We went to the basement where there was a lot of activity, there was a buzz going on, something was happening. Lots of people chatting, quite hostile towards us at first. We asked to see him, we insisted, we said we had a lot to talk about with Mr. Boban. He was having a meeting with some people behind a curtain, the curtain was drawn back, the people left and we got to speak to him. He said: "I have just been made the president of the HDZ Party in Bosnia". We congratulated him, it seemed to be appropriate, polite at least. He congratulated us in turn for having the first exclusive interview with the new president of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina which we were about to have, so we sat down. Stop me if it is a digression, but in parenthesis, I just want to say where Mate Boban at that time stood within the HDZ. The HDZ was the Party founded by President Tudjman of Croatia. He was the leader. The HDZ, BiH -- BH was the Bosnian branch of its sister Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, part of the same pyramid but obviously separated by what Mr. Boban had called "this unfortunate historical circumstance". The President of the Party had until that time been a man Stejpan Kujic. Now, Kujic lived in Sarajevo. He recognised the authority of the Sarajevo government and he was, although not a member of the Government, he was not a member of the ruling Party, he was a sort of, a loyal Croatian opposition or a loyal Croatian slice of what had been the Muslim/Croat alliance, if you like. He was critical of the Government but supported it in the war. Most importantly, he said he believed Bosnian Herzegovina should be one country shared by the three ethnic groups, in which he saw his Party as representing the best interests of the Croats. This was in diametric opposition to what Mr. Boban had outlined to us in August. Unbracket -- not unbracket, forgive me, Mr. Kujic, who I saw later -- who I saw the following year, he recalled that day well, he said it was a putsch, he said he had been kicked out, Boban's people had taken over the Party and it had been on Zagreb's instruction. That is unbracket. We sat down to talk to Mate Boban. This is a briefing I will not forget. He had something to say and he wanted us to repeat it. He started off by talking about the Croatian Community, itself. He said that, and I quote -- notes taken in shorthand by the way: "Not a single Croatian will participate in the Geneva talks [then under way] other than those you see in my company or authorised by my signature. Mate Boban is going to become the voice of the Croats at the Geneva peace talks", which were then in process. As you see, nobody else was going to take part except for his people. He said of the HDZ: "We have our political platform and anyone who disagrees with it will either step down or leave in some other manner." Not much misunderstanding that. He is in charge and there is no dissent. It is becoming a monolith. He then developed his arguments, I remember quizzing him on the point earlier in the year about not recognising the Sarajevo Government or the constitution. I asked him about the army, and what we had been seeing in Mostar, Vitez and Novi Travnik. He said he did not recognise the army of Bosnian Herzegovina either. He called it "a purely Muslim militia", which proved to be true in the long term but was not then. He said the HVO was: "The only effective army in the free territory". The free territory meant all territory not under Serb control, including Tuzla, all places he had not been for a long time. He said the HVO was: "Ready to assume control of Herceg-Bosna." I asked him about Mostar. He said: "Only the HVO can have an armed police in Mostar" -- that did not mean to arrest traffic offenders, to fight units. No Bosnian Army. His last point was at the time, I thought pretty irrelevant, but in retrospect extremely important. He fine-tuned all the stuff about cantons and provinces. He said he thought Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided to three constituent parts and those parts should be sub-divided into nine provinces. This is October 24th. The Geneva talks are under way, Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance were negotiating with parties, but were still three months from publishing what would become called the Vance-Owen Plan. With hindsight, this was an extraordinary remark, because the number of provinces is out by only one, the three constituent parts is bang on. I remember, if I may jump ahead, that when the Vance-Owen Plan was finally published, we joked about whether the author was Lord Owen, Cyrus Vance or Mate Boban, so close was it to his notions, his ideas. Actually, there was a good joke around at that time; what does HVO stand for -- "Harla Vance-Owen", which means, "Thank you, Vance-Owen". So that -- although I did not think much of it at the time -- was rather ironic with hindsight and much written about as well. Coming away from that meeting, I remember we talked about it and we were quite disturbed. Still the man from Reuters. On reflection it was (1), an assumption of absolute authority within the Croatian community, within its polity. It was an assumption of absolute command and authority within the Croatian military, which up until that time, had been -- while the HVO was the mainstream, there had been a number of militias on the outskirts, I mentioned the HOS was the main one. But this was HVO now assuming, as he put it, control of Herceg-Bosna. It was also an assumption of authority and command over his erstwhile allies in the Bosnian Army and on the Muslim side. So we were left really in no doubt that there was now only one chain of command and at the top of it was Mate Boban. There was certainly no room for any dissent; as he made clear, "step down or leave in some other manner"; I do not think anyone would misunderstand that. The other thing, it certainly explained -- the rapid events of the past week were less than a week away from his trip to Travnik, five days away from the first shoot-out in Novi Travnik. It is extraordinary but that is the case. The coherence of his briefing explained the coherence of everything that happened over the past few days. The whole thing had been transformed in those few days. The landscape had been transformed, the alliances had been ruptured and transformed. But the worst fear, and I remember us talking about this, that we had heard this language from the Serbs in eastern Slovonia, around Vukovar and Borovo Selo in the first war, we heard it from the Serbs in the Krajina of Croatia, we heard it from the Croats in some parts of Croatia. Above all, we heard it from the Serbs in the Drina Valley and around Prijedor and Banja Luka. In every one of those instances these were followed by attacks against civilians with the intention of either killing or removing them. I think that is the first time it dawned on us as we left Boban that night: are Muslims supposed to remain in Herceg-Bosna. If so, how? We thought perhaps they probably were not. Those fears were confirmed. The first fears were confirmed horribly quickly. We returned to -- overnight somewhere in northern Croatia, just near the border. We went through the next day, through a little town called Prozor, and it was a Sunday. Everything was apparently normal. We went with the British Army the following day, who were trying to stake out an aid route through to Sarajevo. They were turned back -- oddly enough, not by the Serbs, who were de-sieging Sarajevo, although they might well have been, probably would have been -- but by the Croats who, for some reason, did not want this aid route which would have used tarmac roads through Tarcine, to the east, to work. Then we found out why. We went back up through Prozor on Tuesday, 27th, two days after it had been calm, to find the town a different and terrifying place. Coming up to it, we saw HVO tanks and heavy weapons were vetted into the ground near a place called Romboci. Coming down on the tarmac road to Prozor was written in huge writing, fresh paint, English "Cro territory". Got into the main street and every other, or thereabouts, building in the main street had been burned out -- Apologies to the interpreters. The main street of Prozor, which had been full of people having a coffee on Sunday, every other building, say one in three at minimum, had been burnt out or destroyed in some way. There were signs of shelling. There were signs of heavy gunfire and small arms fire. There was looting going on, there were gangs of soldiers around the streets, helping themselves to the contents of the shops and the furniture. The oddity, I had never seen this before, was that every soldier -- some had HVO patches on, some did not, but every one had a red ribbon tied to his epaulette. I had never seen this before, I did not know what it meant. As you come out of Prozor, we did not want to stop to ask, we were the only car on the road. It was strange because in the outskirts of the -- behind what I think is probably the Croatian side, kids were playing, sitting on walls, messing about on the streets. By the time we got to the centre the place was completely empty. We did not want to stop. When you leave the town you go past a mosque on the left and the road turns round to the left and starts to climb a hill. That is what I took to be the Muslim quarter or mainly Muslim quarter, probably mixed, but where the mosque was. The minaret was not down but it was damaged. More importantly, most of the buildings around it were damaged either by shell fire or more usually by burning, again a sign of small arms fire. There was a dead horse lying in the road. No other sign of human bodies or anything, just this dead horse. Up the hill, and on the top of the hill, there is a ski chalet mountain building which had been transformed into a garrison. The place was crawling with soldiers --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, HVO, but they have this ribbon on which I do not understand now, all wearing this ribbon on their epaulettes. As we drove on, new road blocks in what had previously been secure allied territory and bunkering down either side of the road which proceeds to Gornji Vakuf. There is a movement going on, this is a push, this is not free-booting around a town looting, this is a military operation and a quick and efficient one at that. But, the most important thing is that apparently the Muslims appeared to have gone from the town. I would like to just, if I may -- stop me if you think it is irrelevant -- Prozor has very important strategic significance. It is -- Prozor means "window". Prozor is, as it were, the window -- it is the gateway between Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. It is in a dip in a valley. Prozor, if you want to control Central Bosnia, as we now know Mate Boban and the HVO very much wanted to do, Prozor was your first stop up the line. Whoever controls Prozor is the keeper of the gate from Herzegovina, where the petrol is, where the access to the coast is, where some attempt at normal life is, and Central Bosnia. There is a second, even more important reason why Prozor was strategically important to a coherent military operation. It was the pivotal point on what we were calling "Route Diamond", what the British Army -- the UN -- British UN army was calling Route Diamond. Route Diamond was a road being built out of a track by the Royal Engineers running from Tomislavgrad, Duvno on some maps, up through Prozor, Gornji Vakuf to Vitez. It was the aid lifeline for Central Bosnia. The tarmac roads from the east through Mostar and the left through Livno were exposed to Serb artillery. For some months now they had been building this road since August -- what other people called "salvation road". If you controlled Route Diamond, you controlled the aid tap into Central Bosnia. There were even times when control of Route Diamond also meant control of all aid into the capital of Sarajevo, where hundreds of thousands of people, as everybody knows, were still entrapped, because other routes into Sarajevo were closed and you had to get up Route Diamond even to go down through Kiseljak and a Serb checkpoint at Ilidza into the capital. Prozor was, if you like, the bone in the throat, of this aid respiratory apparatus. One man's aid route is also another man's military supply route. The HVO needed to control Route Diamond, Prozor, ergo Route Diamond, it seemed to anyone with a half a brain, because if you controlled the aid tap you also had a road up, you could run your troops, tanks, anything else you wanted into Central Bosnia. It made -- it was militarily obvious that the Croatians needed to control Prozor. However, all this was for talking about another time. We did not want to go back through Prozor, it was getting dark, we decided to risk it, go through Novi Travnik -- which was thoroughly unpleasant because there was shooting going on -- to Travnik, where at least we knew we could get a bed, which we did. We want to the commander of the Bosnian Army in Travnik, a man called Haso Ribo, who was usually quite a sort of genial guy. He was angry and he was mad. I had never seen him before like that, never seen him like that since. He said, and we wrote this down and transmitted it later on, he said: "All we want to do is fight with these people against our common enemy, the Serbs". He said this in rather sort of a statuesque way. There were not many journalists hanging around Travnik that night. He said: "I appeal to whoever is giving these orders to stop". He said: "My reports are that 5,000 Muslims are now missing from Prozor. We do not know where they are, it is night-time". Well, next day we wake up. Only one thing to do, fairly obvious, try to find the 5,000 Muslims. Back down from Gornji Vakuf to Prozor. They are not there. We set off along a road from Prozor towards the town of Jablanica. It was raining very heavily. This is now the 28th October, only eight days after Mate Boban's visit to Travnik, and seven days after the shoot-out, of one bullet, at a petrol station. We set out on this road. We found the first -- we set out along the road out of Prozor towards Jablanica and found the first stragglers on the road, women and children. One woman in her bedroom slippers, I recall, in the rain. We stopped the car, got out and said: "who are you and what has happened?" They said they had been spending the night looking for caves in which to hide, because groups of soldiers were out killing people who were wandering around the woods and the countryside. We were taking these notes when an old minicab appeared and a man got out and we said we were journalists, he said to -- some of, he could not fit them all, he said, "Get in my taxi and you people follow me". Actually we put some of the people in our car as well. We drove behind the minicab. He took a track off the road up into the hills. This is to the east of Prozor, south-east of Prozor. We drove quite a long way behind him and as the countryside opened up -- I will never forget this, it was an extraordinary sight -- there were people moving around in fields, sitting by the road, in the doorways of little houses, and here were the Muslims of Prozor wandering around the mountains. We stopped and interviewed people. There was one woman called Nadia who said that the shelling -- first of all her Croat neighbours had begun to leave without explaining why over the weekend. Then on -- I am afraid it was either the Sunday or the Monday night, I did not take a note of that. I think it was the Sunday night -- the Monday night sorry, going into Tuesday dawn, but it was not clear whether she meant Sunday going into Monday dawn, the shelling had begun at night and they spent the night in the cellar. At dawn soldiers came into the town shooting and some people had been killed. She had managed to run away in her night-dress along a ditch. A soldier said that he had seen bodies being loaded up on to a cart and towed by tractor out of the town and he -- the same guy, his name was Senad, I think, he said he had been in the Bosnian Army and he said: "but we had accepted the flag of Herceg-Bosna in our town, we accepted their stamps on our documents" -- this is a country where everything is rubber-stamped several times. Still this happened. So left them -- I think we gave them our petrol, as I recall. Left them to head back through Prozor, just outside the town a car was -- had not been there before, was on the side of the road, parked. Bullets in it, no sign of anybody. Just clearly had been shot at as it drove down the road. Did not like the look of that. As we drove back through the town, the men were still helping themselves to the contents of shops and making sort of home videos of their handy work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, were these HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody HVO, and still with this ribbon. The track, which is all Route Diamond was at that time, back to Tomislavgrad, there were three or four trucks full of soldiers, all with the epaulette, HVO patches, all singing, they had drink on board, all songs I knew by that time, songs of the old Ustasha, from the Second World War. So it was interesting, here was these people who came up the line from Tomislavgrad; they were now going back -- some of them, plenty still left up on the hills, I suppose maybe the local people remained. In Tomislavgrad, the atmosphere was extraordinary. Troops everywhere. We went to the Tomislavgrad Hotel to use the telephone, where also you had been able to stay, but now could not, but we managed to bargain a room and use of the phone because the ECMM, European Community Monitoring Mission man was working there out of the hotel. We told him what had happened. He was insistent that we meet with the commander of the HVO in Tomislavgrad, a man called Zelig. He came down. He was an old man. All I can remember about this long dinner was that every now and then there would be a rasp of machine-gun fire out in the street and we were slightly alarmed. He said: "Do not worry, only night games". These were the celebrations going on. He produced these maps and rather wildly took us at great length through the significance of each map. It was a map of Croatia, down the centuries. He described in great detail each map, celebrating that in which Croatia expanded and lamenting that in which Croatia shrunk. The last map, number 12, was captioned "future Croatian Federation" and showed all, if not most, of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be part of Croatia. He was very excited about this. Our attention was immediately distracted by the next disaster, which was the fall of the town of Jajce. 40,000 people came over the mountains and hills under fire. The Serbs had taken Jajce. It was an extraordinary day, they came to Travnik, it was like something out of Tolstoy that day, with horses and carts and sheep, a defeated army. For the purposes of this incident, the interesting incident that day was that the soldiers from what had been an allied defence of Jajce, of Muslims and Croats, were told to report to their respective headquarters in Travnik, HVO or Bosnian Army. We went to both. At the Bosnian Army headquarters there were a lot of Croats reporting. They had a patch on their arms which I had not seen before, which was -- which had the lilies of Bosnia in the top right-hand quarter and the chequer-board of Croatia in the bottom corner, left-hand corner of the shield, a short of gesture of alliance, if you like. These men were absolutely furious. They said: "We could have defended Jajce". They were saying -- rightly or wrongly, I have no way of judging, this: "There has been a deal between Boban and Karadzic, we were pulled off the lines, there was no reason for us to be pulled off the lines. We could have hung on". I have no way of judging whether this was true or whether the defence of Jajce, as is also possible, had simply become insupportable and they decided to concede the town. There were the soldiers saying: "I am not going to fight for Mate Boban against my Muslim friends any more". I thought that was quite interesting. That is the last I had to do with this particular element of the story in 1992, but it goes on. I next went back into the area in late January 1993. This was to make a film for the BBC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, before you go into that, in the Prozor area in October of 1992, were you familiar prior to that time with a HOS checkpoint at Romboci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court about your observations after your conversation with Boban concerning that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This takes us back to that eventful week of October 20th onwards in 1992. Checkpoint etiquette was crucial in Bosnia, you had to know how to play it. Everybody had checkpoints, you were going through them all the time. We were driving -- I was driving, with whoever I was working with, a rather easily-identified English, British registered Citroen car which had been comandeered from the literary editor, company car, for the war effort. It had a Union Jack on the bonnet of the car. It was quite well known by some of the men manning the road blocks, at least the regular ones because they thought it was funny, and would joke about how no-one would want to steal the car because the steering wheel was on the wrong side -- nor do I blame them. There was one checkpoint just before Romboci, south-west of Prozor, which was run by the HOS, not by the HVO. It had "HOS" written on the side of the little hut they had and they were always wearing a black T-shirt to distinguish themselves from the HVO. It was around -- it was during that week, the week before Prozor, during the Novi Travnik -- it was either one of the Prozor journeys or it was the Novi Travnik return journey when, during that week, when we got to that road block and they all had new HVO uniforms with HVO patches on the side. We joked about it with them. I said: "What happened to HOS, no HOS any more?" There was joking about the smart new uniforms and they had not got the black T-shirts -- this was mainly the translator having the jokes, not me. We knew the guys, they had been HOS, they were not any more, they were HVO. That was the actually last time I saw any other militia. In the summer of 92 there had been a plethora of these militias. By the end of October they had gone. That HOS checkpoint was the only one that seemed to survive into October. They, in the end to the general mirth of everybody, had gone to the HVO and had their new uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move to January, Mr. Vulliamy, by the end of October, you had observed what had happened in Vitez and in the Hotel Vitez. You had observed what happened in Mostar in the disarmament order as well as the comments of HVO command. You observed what happened in Prozor. You observed what happened with the transformation of the HOS unit to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had you concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that everything that Mate Boban had predicted at his first and second meeting was being implemented with great efficiency. It was coherent, no dissent, everything going to plan. There was only one chain of command and it was working, people was obeying the orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue on, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: January 1993, I go back to make a film. This is working for the BBC, which is easier, because you do not have to drive a Citroen car, you get an armoured vehicle, and we needed it, because the landscape had changed. Route Diamond was now shut. We had to use an alternative route up country through Kiseljak and there were new road blocks all along the road between Kiseljak, up towards Vitez through Busovaca. Mostly HVO, but also Bosnian Army. At certain points -- two anyway, at least two points along the way. There were burnt-out houses along the road in territory controlled by both sides, which had not been the case before. There was a war going on. There was tit-for-tat ethnic cleansing immediately visible before you started asking questions. Before we could get past Vitez we -- before we could get past Vitez we went to Travnik, a frightening journey back, cars shot off the road, we were shot at Busovaca. It was a very, very menacing atmosphere indeed, that which began in October had descended or progressed or however you want to say. This film was about Muslims in Travnik and does not concern us particularly, except that there was one episode that I think was very important. The commander of the HVO in Travnik had changed. It was not the young man Prokrajcic any more, but it was another man who appeared to share his views. This man was called Filip Filipovic. Now, we are many months into the war between the army and the HVO, but Filipovic would have none of it. Mate Boban was not getting much luck in Travnik. We had a camera, nobody had had a camera in Travnik for a fairly long time, I think, at least not for any length of time. Commander Filipovic said that he had daily contact with his Muslim opposite, whose name was Ahmed Kulenovic. He wanted us to go up Mount Vlasic just outside Travnik, with him and the Muslim commander Kulenovic, because he was interested in the viability of attacking the top of the mountain on which the Serbs held an radio antennae which had telecommunications over all the area, which controlled telecommunications over all the area. Filipovic wanted to take it and knew he could only do that with help of the Muslims. He wanted us to film him walking up the mountain to within just under the noses of the Serbs, a very dangerous walk, with the commander of the Bosnian Army. We talked a lot about it on the way up. This was the third time I heard Colonel Blaskic's name mentioned. I had heard it mentioned -- I had not met him. I had heard it mentioned twice by one officer in the Cheshire Regiment and a man from the UNHCR when they had been talking about a cease-fire agreement that they had been obliged to sign by Colonel Blaskic. They did not particularly want to sign it, but he and his Muslim counterpart, who I think was Hadzihuseinovic, I think, obliged him to sign it. They were both uneasy. Anyway, this was the third time I heard his name, because Colonel Filipovic -- I think it was Colonel, maybe Major, Filipovic cursed Mate Boban and Colonel Blaskic. He said: "They are putting me in a position I do not want to be in. They are making me" -- this was the expression -- "walk the edge of a knife". By that, I think he meant that -- if you fell it would be extremely painful, but that he was either going to have to go over one side of the knife and join in with the Muslims -- thereby disobeying orders and renouncing his orders -- or he was going to have to fall the other side of the knife, adopt a hostile relationship to his Muslim counterpart and do something he did not want to do, for reasons that were personal and, as he was showing us only too clearly, military as well. He chose this little PR exercise, this little walk with the Muslim counterpart on television on television, under the noses of the Serbs, to say this. I, with hindsight, find that very interesting. There was another point that was interesting about that time. Despite the hardships -- lack of water, electricity and so on -- work had begun on a telephone system now. Now I am going to jump ahead of myself a bit, this takes about a year to complete. Around this time from the post offices in Central Bosnia you could begin to start making telephone calls, land-line, non-satellite telephone calls. I admit that in January, February and now we are into the February with the Filipovic episode, it is mid to late February by now, I do not know the date, I am afraid. In February 1993, it is difficult to try to make the telephone calls. Within a few months you can phone any Croat-held town, to Kiseljak or Emotske, but you cannot phone Zenica, you cannot phone Sarajevo. The significance of this, I thought, was that the area code, the country code, although we were well into Bosnia, is 385; the country code for Bosnia-Herzegovina is 387. That was not it. It was an exact mirror of what was happening in the Serb areas where the country code is 381, which is Yugoslavia. These little bits of infrastructure seemed to be important in a place where there was almost no normal life going on. Also, despite the hardships, they had embossed, nice and expensively manufactured number plates, Herceg-Bosna number plates. Every car which -- they used to just paint out the red star of Yugoslavia, but they now had their special number plates with a proper indented crest of Herceg-Bosna on all cars in the area. January to February 1993. I thought that was both impressive but rather ominous. It was not until the following summer I was back to Bosnia, after that. During that time, the Vance-Owen Plan had been eagerly signed to by the Croats -- for obvious reasons, I do not think I need go over that again -- in my view, incomprehensibly by the Muslims, had been rejected by the Serbs and some of the worst violence in Central Bosnia had taken place. I remember reading about how the HVO had unilaterally said: we are setting up our interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan anyway, and Herceg-Bosna was effectively up and running as an institution by the time I returned, and this was in July 1993. I was only very briefly in Central Bosnia this time, but if I said the landscape had transformed between October and late January and February, it had transformed more so now. There was fighting almost everywhere. Bugonjo was under heavy attack -- at least, they were fighting for Bugonjo. Gornji Vakuf was a battlefield with the front-line running right through the town. There was even a sniper from the Bosnian Army on the hill above where we were staying in Vitez next to the British base and the sniper used to shoot down into the garden at us when we were trying to read. This is the only time I met Colonel Blaskic, now General. I wanted by now -- by now our passes had -- a pass that you used to have that was good for Sarajevo, Mostar, Split and Zagreb, was invalid. You had to have a special pass for Mostar, HVO pass for Mostar, which I did not have, to get past a village called Nova Bila on the way to Travnik where I needed to go. They said: "You cannot come, you will have to go to Hotel Vitez". At the Hotel Vitez they said: "Only Colonel Blaskic can give you a special paper". I hung around for a while and I asked him if he could give me such a letter. I fully understand he had other things to think about and gave this half a second's attention. The aide to whom I was referred did not gave me the paper, but it was possible to get through, because you simply got up at 5 o'clock in the morning when there was no-one of the road blocks to get in. Anyway, that was the only time I met him and I fully understand him not wasting his time with my pass. The matters of urgency at this point, though, were elsewhere in Herceg-Bosna. There were reports of ethnic cleansing on a dramatic scale going on in the Mostar area and of fighting, severe fighting within Mostar itself. We went back to Mr. Boban's headquarters in Grude. He had moved again, now into a sort of industrial premises on the outskirts of town. We asked to go to Mostar, east Mostar, the Muslim quarter as well. For access, the answer was: "No. No-one would get through there for another two months". We asked to go to a place called Capljina. We were told: "No". We said: "Why no?" -- it is not Mr. Boban, he would not see us, it is his spokesman, George, Canadian, I do not know the second name, I am afraid, I will just have to call him "Canadian George". He said we no, we could not go to Capljina because it was an action zone. "How come an action zone?", we said, "It is 10 miles from the front-line". "Never mind, you cannot go there". Obviously we have to go to Capljina. If you are not allowed to go there, there must be a reason. We got turned back at the checkpoints. There we had a rather good idea. We got the translators, a guy from the Washington Post and I. We got the translator's beat-up old car, lounged around in the back reading Croatian newspapers and a flysheet that had been handed out in Grude, made a point of putting our feet out of the car and spitting out of the window. This was enough to get you waved through. So we got into the town. This was frightening and familiar from the Serb days, the days around Prijedor and Banja Luka. There were troops all over the streets. It was not like Prozor but there were bombed out and burnt-out shops all over the main street, selected houses destroyed, burnt out, graffiti painted on them. We found an old man, the only civilian was an old man and the translator asked him what is going on. He said: "My sons have been taken away". Then a lady appeared and pointed to the mosque, so we went to the mosque. There was the imam with some very distressed women. He told us that since July 4th, and we are now by the way on July 18th 1993, since July 4th, the steady apprehension of all the Muslim men in the town had begun and was now more or less complete. They had gone. And the women were starting to be moved and those women who remained, including those who were in the company of the imam, did not know where their men folk were. One of them said that her husband had been taken while playing for his soccer team, practising for his soccer team. Others said that they had been taken from the front-lines, while they had been fighting with the HVO. In this area -- the Bosnian Army did not really exist, only the HVO and a lot of Muslims were still fighting, unbelievably, in the HVO, against the Serbs. They had been apprehended on the front-lines and taken -- they did not know where, but the women had heard of the names of two camps: Dretelj and Gabela. They said they tried to find, to locate their husbands, to go to the places but they had not been able to go to the places. This was all horribly familiar. I am not here to testify on what was happening around Prijedor and Banja Luka the previous year but it was the pattern. You arrived in these places, the womenfolk were distraught, the men had gone, they did not know where, word of camps, the whole thing was utterly depressing and familiar. Back to Mate Boban's headquarters and Canadian George. Mr. Boban does not want to see us again. We say we have just been to Capljina and Canadian George says: "Impossible, you are not allowed into Capljina". We said: "Tough, we have been there, what the hell is going on? Where is Dretelj, what is Dretelj?" He said: "You cannot go to Dretelj, it is in an action zone." We said: "Come on, it is miles from anywhere. What about Gabela, what is that?" "You cannot there either, that is another action zone"; Gabela is down on the Croatian border. Anyway, so we then returned to the UNHCR and asked them more about this. This was the UNHCR office in Medzugorje where the nearest hotels were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we go into this briefing, Mr. President, are you nodding to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we will take a break now. We will resume 15 minutes. (4.10 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court is now in session. Please bring in the accused. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Vulliamy, we were just about to move to the UNHCR briefing in Medugorje. Prior to that, if I might ask about the trip to Capljina. When you were there, you said there were troops in the area, in the town, those were HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can continue to tell the court the story from the time you go to the briefing? Again, give us some time frames here on dates, when it took place in Medugorje with UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is July 18th, 1993. We have spent the best part of the afternoon in Capljina, talking to these women. There is always the details that stay with you. I remember one woman describing how the HVO guys had come around to take all the jewellery and money and anything they wanted from her house. She had her money in her knickers but, as she said, they found it in the end. Capljina, no Dretelj, cannot go, but there are camps out there. We went that night to the office of the UNHCR in Medugorje, where you could get a bed. There were two people there, one of them -- they gave us a very interesting briefing. They said yes, they had heard about what they called a mesh of camps, to which they thought 10,000 or so men had been transported. They confirmed the names, Dretelj and Gabela and added another, Rodoc, outside Mostar. They then told us an extraordinary story about a meeting they had been obliged to go to in the Croatian coastal town of Makarska, the previous week. They had been told there by the Herceg-Bosna authorities that what they wanted to do was to deport some 50,000 men to third countries via a transit camp that they planned to establish at a town called Ljubuski near by --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 50,000 Bosnian men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Muslim men from Herceg-Bosna. Through a transit camp capable of holding 50,000 people in Ljubuski nearby. The UNHCR officials told us how amazed they were by this notion, but not as amazed as they were by the fact that Mate Granic, the Croatian Foreign Minister from Zagreb, Croatia proper, was at this meeting and said his Government would cooperate with the UNHCR if they wished to become involved in this plan. This was also familiar from what was now a year ago, because when we were covering the Serb violence against the Croats and the Muslims in north western Bosnia, what Radovan Karadzic and his people had succeeded in doing was to put the UNHCR -- and this is what we thought, and this is what they said, and told us again that night in Medzugorje -- in a grotesque Catch-22 situation, whereby you could either cooperate with the ethnic cleansing as a full participant and help these people achieve their aims, or you could allow these men to fester in camps, the existence of which you knew about, but into which the Red Cross -- the International Red Cross -- was still not allowed to go. Hobson's choice, as we say in English; choice between two evils. The UNHCR in Medugorje was at that time caught in exactly the same appalling dilemma as that which their colleagues had been caught in Prijedor and Banja Luka during the tempest of violence there. There was no end to that conversation. There was an interesting little code although; we asked about Capljina and the mayor -- who we had been unable to find and did not want to spend too much time looking for -- they said his name was Pero Markovic and told us that they had seen a document but did not have it -- I stress that -- a document which he had been the author of, which suggested a -- what he called -- breeding programme for Muslims, arguing that Muslim women in the town not be admitted to hospital to have children because they tended to breed what he called -- I am quoting the UNHCR "antisocial and antiauthoritarian elements" when they gave birth to children. With that, I left Bosnia for what I hoped would be the summer to write a book, but my plan was cut short towards the end of August, when a convoy -- the first convoy -- got into east Mostar and, sometime around then, the first television cameras too. The scenes that I saw on the television were appalling and there was nothing for it but to go back and to go to east Mostar. Back to Medjugorje and there were two matters of urgency, requiring attention: east Mostar but also Dretelj. Amazingly, it was now September and no-one had been to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dates -- I think it is the second week of the month. I am not quite sure what day I arrived in Medjugorje, but it is fairly early on, around the second week of the month. Dretelj was still there, it was still uninspected. The Red Cross had not even been in there. But, there had been articles in newspapers about the first prisoners released from Gabela and Rodoc. According to a report in my paper by a colleague, these men were being sent naked across the no-man's-land into their own territory at Jablanica and shots fired -- I think actually over their heads -- as they were scrambling, naked, down these tracks. I do not know if anyone was killed, but that was the report, and so Dretelj became a matter of urgency. I went to Grude. Canadian George -- again apologies for the lack of a surname -- "Want to see Mate Boban." "Mate Boban does not want to see you". "Want to go to Dretelj". "Do not be silly, you asked that a couple months ago, no." Went to stay the night in Grude, wanted to try again in the morning; went back in the morning. Mr. Boban did not want to see. In came Slobodan Praljak, a face we all knew; he was the commander of the HVO. We though: Well, let us ask him. To my absolute amazement, he said, "Yes" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this conversation with Praljak, had there been any articles in the newspaper from President Tudjmann to individuals in Herceg-Bosna concerning these camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to say that. The reason why I think he said "Yes" is because that morning in a paper, Slobodan Dalmacija, I think, although I do not recall exactly which one, there was a front page story which the translator read. It was very interesting. It said that President Tudjman of Zagreb had written a letter to Mr. Boban insisting that he "take all measures to implement humanitarian law in the camps". After two months since the establishment of these camps, this seemed strange, except that what was around, on the diplomatic level, was that Britain and the United States were threatening Zagreb with sanctions if the Bosnian Croats did not comply with international law over these camps. Croatia at that time needed sanctions like a hole in the head. There was, I think, some pressure on Boban; there was a panic in Zagreb. I know that the Americans were particularly pushing that if Croatia did not clean up the act in Bosnia -- in Herceg-Bosna, sanctions would be debated at the UN. So, I suspect that is why Praljak, to my amazement, to my colleague's amazement, said: "Yes, you can go to Dretelj". Certainly, the secretary who typed out the order paper, for which we asked, was pretty amazed, as was the century when we arrived a little later at Dretelj. It was deja vu for me because I had not known, when we were talking about Dretelj, that this was the HOS camp I had visited when it was full of Serbs almost a year ago, in August 1992, on the day I first met Mate Boban, in fact. Anyway, here we were in Dretelj a year later, this time the prisoners Muslim. In we went. We were greeted by the commander of the camp, a man called Tomo Sakota and the tour began in the hospital quarters. A euphemism. It was a room in the baking heat of what was a very hot summer. The men were two to a bed, rough beds, under blankets. Bones protruding from shoulders; dry parchment skin, hollow eyes, watered eyes, weeping sores; very ill. They were being tended by three Muslim doctors, who were prisoner doctors, who said that they had been trying to treat malnutrition, broken ribs and some men had died from natural causes and they made gestures as to indicate this was intense heat without proper hydration. Our tour continued. The rules of engagement were established by the commander. We were allowed to interview prisoners only in his presence and through our interpreter, and he had to be present. There were to be no interviews outside his earshot in German or in English, one to one. We went into some sheds, single-storey sheds in which, during my previous visit in August 1992 had been full of Serb women, when it was a HOS camp. Now it was an HVO camp and occupied by Muslim men. They were so cramped that they were not able to lay down. They were crouching or squatting on the floor in the heat and they had hung their little plastic bags of belongings on the rafters above so they would not take up any space on the floor. We were able to break the rules quite quickly and easily by fanning out so there were -- there were three of us in the party, the BBC and Daily Telegraph were along. We fanned out, so we could pick up information independently. I spoke to a disc jockey from a place called Stolac who told me during the summer the doors were locked for up to 72 hours at a time during which they spent a lot of effort trying to get excreta out of the windows just above head height so the smell would not be too intolerable. They would be obliged -- there would be no water or food during that period that the doors were shut and they would be obliged to drink their own urine in pursuit of hydration. We continued on to a bit of the camp I had not seen before, which the HOS had hidden from us. This was two hangars built into mounds opposite each other with a bit of ground in between, they were effectively underground, going into the ground with metal sliding doors. The doors were open, obviously for our visit, and we began to wander round. By now the rules had rather sort of fallen apart. We were surprisingly free to talk to people. They said that thing had improved a bit since Mr. Sakota had arrived, that the worst treatment had been earlier in the summer. One time, in particular, when the doors were locked, again up to 72 hours at a time -- no chance of removing excreta, this time, of course, because they were in pitch black and there were no windows. Again, drinking their own urine. They described a night during which the guards had had a booze up and starting firing their machine-guns through the doors; estimates of those killed during that night were 10 to 12, and there was evidence to backup what they said because there were bullet holes in the door and the metal very clearly gnarled inwards and pock marks across the back wall. There were other stories of maltreatment, but the most interesting thing concerned the visit of the Red Cross, which we found out at that time had happened the previous day. Now the men were in disagreement with each other as to whether conditions had improved when Commander Sakota had taken over, a few weeks before somewhere in July or in the past few days, opinions varied. One man told us that 120 of the prisoners in the worst condition had been removed before the Red Cross had arrived and we asked Commander Sakota about this. He said: "No, but" -- this is an odd defence -- "Mate Granic, the Croatian Foreign Minister, telephoned me two days before the Red Cross was due to come into the camp and asked me to" -- and I use his words "make these peoples' lives a little easier", in preparation for their visit. The tour of the camp continued -- very humiliating eating conditions, men made to line up in a group of, I think, between 20 and 30, to jog across a stretch of land, collect their watery stew in a metal bowl, crouch on the ground under armed guard while eating, wash the bowls, return to the line and back to the hangar. I was particularly struck by the reluctance of a lot of the prisoners to come out into the area of the hangar, which was lighter, towards the door; just sitting at the back in the darkness, as though they were blind. When we asked them why they were not taking advantage of the opportunity of the open door, they said: "We are not really allowed out anyway, and we are too scared to go out into the yard". Well, that was Dretelj. We left and -- a little episode on the road, we took a shortcut back to Medzugorje and as we did so a car came up alongside us with HVO number plates and side-swiped me. It was not very pleasant. It did not push me into the ditch, it did not stay with me like it might do in the movies, but it gave me a good bash on the side, overtook and carried on. Coming from the camp, a clear message of what the guards thought of our visit, I expect. Bosnia was comparative nightmares, sort of difficult to measure but I think one has to try to measure these things if it is useful. I had been to a number of camps over on the other side, on the Serb side; Omarska, Trnopolje. I did not go to Keraterm, I went to a prison called Kula, near Sarajevo. It is grotesque, but I will try to evaluate Dretelj on a scale for you. I think it is fair to say that it was -- Trnopolje was in north-western Bosnia near Prijedor.
