I think it was probably on a par with, if not marginally worse, than Trnopolje , but nowhere near as bad as Omarska. This is not a language I particularly enjoy, but it was a very bad place. It was nothing like Omarska, I would not want to make a comparison to Omarska, which was the nearest Bosnia had to a death camp, not a word I like to use, because of the echoes, but Dretelj was I think as bad as the Croats meted out and, measured in Serb terms -- not an exercise I think is particularly justifiable, but if it helps -- it was as bad as, if not slightly worse than Trnopolje. The UNHCR was the next port of call, for obvious reasons. The Red Cross did not want to talk about it, and that is their prerogative. The UNHCR said: "Yes, Dretelj, we can confirm everything you have been talking about from what we have heard, although we have not been in". Commander Sakota had put the numbers of internees at 1400, the UNHCR said that sounded about right but that earlier in the summer there had been between 2,000 and 2,500 men in that camp. Honestly, the idea of those conditions being worsened by a crowding factor of -- what would it be -- 40 per cent or whatever, was pretty horrifying. Now, these Herceg-Bosna authorities were pretty hard to get to see nowadays, but -- certainly they made little effort to talk to us. The next day something quite extraordinary happened: they came to us en masse, the press was that holed up in Medzugorje at the time and a platoon of Herceg-Bosna leadership descended on the town, for our convenience, to hold a press conference. I had never known anything like that happen before or since. Boban was not there, nor was Praljak. The star turn was Kresimir Zubak. Then I think -- he was introduced as Vice President of the HVO. I do not know how to interpret that. He later became President of the Federation. He insisted that the internment of these men was an "imperative", his word, because Muslims of a militarily-capable age had to be, as he put it, "isolated". He conceded, however, that the provisions of the Geneva Conventions had not been met in these camps but excused himself by saying that this was because of the numbers which had been interned in them at such speed. We asked him what was the excuse for this maltreatment. He gave the time-honoured answer that no order had been given to maltreat prisoners but maltreatment may have resulted from the actions of -- he put it -- "irresponsible individuals", but that no report had been received by HVO command of the maltreatment of prisoners. For what my opinion is worth, given that Mate Granic had been on the phone from Zagreb asking them to clean up the act and given that these camps had been established for two months and the Red Cross refused access, I did not believe him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What do you mean by "clean up the act"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I was referring to Commander Sakota's report of his phone call from Foreign Minister Mate Granic in Zagreb asking him to -- and his report of Granic's word was to "make these peoples' lives a little easier". Sorry, I did not mean to paraphrase in slang. With Zubak at that event was a man called Barislav Pusic, who introduced himself as the Herceg-Bosna president for prisoner exchange. He said that he thought that the camp perfectly met what he called "international principles" and said that if the hangars were good enough for JNA soldiers, why were they not good enough for Muslim prisoners; did not even bother to get into the argument about the fact that JNA soldiers would have been on beds and that they were not locked in the hangars. Dretelj had been a barracks before the war. On to the other pressing matter of Mostar. Dretelj answered the question: where had the men gone? Where were the women and children? The answer was horrific, east Mostar. The Spanish had left Mostar the day before -- the Spanish UNPROFOR contingent had left the town, I would say fled the town. The day before a Croat offensive had begun, on May 9th. They were in Medzugorje as well and running a twice weekly or maybe every other day patrol into town and taking passengers, not many volunteers. Again, I am forced to make comparisons for your benefit, if you think it is useful. All these sieges were dreadful. Sarajevo was famously dreadful. Srebrenica, Sepa -- God only knows what they were like, could not get there through the worst of it. But east Mostar was one of the most frightening places I went to during the entire war. Only the Muslim half of a little village called Bosanska Krupa, which was being besieged by the Serbs at close range was worse. Mostar was far worse than Sarajevo. As a brain surgeon who had made his way to help at the pitiful hospital, readily conceded, he had come from Sarajevo and he said that Mostar was that bad because of "the concentration of wounded people, women and children". The population of the little Muslim pocket on the east side of the Neretva River, which is basically just a main street with a little village called Blagaj south and a few tower blocks at the north, a bit like old Beirut, and some criss-crossed streets off it down to the river, that is about it. The population of that pocket had been about 10,000 when the siege began in May 1993. By the time we got there in September, the population was estimated at about 50,000. Of the increase, were large numbers of elderly people, women and children. Basically, herded in there, across the no-man's-land of Blagaj to the south and across the bridge into an artillery shooting gallery. By the time we got there, 400 people had died in the then subterranean hospital alone, that is excluding those killed on the streets. The man who was trying to run the hospital, told us that he had taken 50 direct tank hits from the other side, although of the -- of the river, although his roof was clearly marked with a Red Cross. The damage had been done mainly to his medicine store which, perhaps rather stupidly, had been in the attic. Carpenters who had tried to repair the roof had been shot at by snipers and had been forced to cease work. There was no water, people had to go to the river to try and get it. The day before we arrived, a mother and her two children had been killed trying to get water out of the river by an anti-aircraft missile fired straight at them. The cross streets were so dangerous that they had built a little sort of main road running around through what was left of peoples' houses. So that you left the main road, at the most dangerous junction and literally were walking through peoples' kitchens, bathrooms, front rooms, through a sort of maze of masonry. It was quite extraordinary; the whole town was walking through these peoples' houses. A women had set up a hairdressing business. You could get your hair cut for a cigarette. I think we paid a couple of packets, but it was a good hair cut. I will limit myself to conditions in Mostar and you can question me if you like further. The European Union at that time had tried to suggest that Mostar be divided between the two communities; Muslim on the east and Croatia to the west. Mr. Boban had been quoted on the radio saying: "No question of Mostar being divided; it is the capital of Herceg-Bosna and only that." One little detail, the Croats had put large amplifiers on the other side of the river which were blaring out a mixture of heavy metal music and old Ustasha songs, which you could hear audibly on the other side. Two purposes, I supposed: listen to this dreadful racket, it will drive you crazier than you are already; but also we have electricity, ha, ha, ha. I have only one more thing to talk about; one more episode. This is February the following year, 1994, when I went back to east Mostar. I met Mate Boban at Split airport -- sorry, at Zagreb airport on the way down to Split. I was with a colleague from the Washington Post, to whom we did talk, he knew who I was, did not want to talk to me very much, except during the conversation, we asked about Mostar and he said: "Mostar will never be divided. It is the capital of Herceg-Bosna." By now, the UNHCR, in Medzugorje were running arm and armoured vehicle into the pocket and a remarkable man, called Jerry Hume, was taking passengers. Greeted like a sort of saviour by the people as he got out of the vehicle when we arrived. He later died soon after of cancer. I think he probably realised it did not really matter which way he went, whether it was cancer or east Mostar; he was going to go anyway. He was a great man. Anyway enough. We got to Mostar again. The first thing Jerry Hume wanted to do was to go and inspect some medical supplies at a new hospital he was hoping to establish. As we arrived, they began opening fire on us from the other side of the river, anti-aircraft, ground to ground, again, and the medicines caught fire. When the fire engine -- that is to say a car with buckets of river water in it -- came to try to put out the fire, they started shooting at that as well. We spent most of the time, three days, in a cellar while the shells came in. It is a very rough estimate, and I always hate numbers in this war, but I think about 1 in 40 people in that pocket were killed. So far as I can gather, the casualties were something around 1,000, if not a little over, dead and obviously many more wounded, a disproportionate number of women and children among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This number is between May and February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is May 9th right up through to February 1994, so you stood a 1 in 40 chance of living. We were in the cellar most of the time, at the entrance to which was a little vase for an Italian film crew that had been killed by a mortar some weeks before which they tended with flowers, which was a nice touch, I thought. Otherwise it was a cat and mouse game. You had to stop at the corner of a road that gave you a sight line of the other side of the river, run, crack, crack, other side, carry on the down the road that way. I made a trip across the river. Unbelievably, there was a two-block promontory on the west side of the river that the Muslims still held. The bridge, the famous arched bridge of Mostar had by now been destroyed by the Croatian gunners and a metal bridge had been built to replace it, across which you had to run. It sort of bounced up at you; quite frightening. You got shot at as you ran. Over on the other side were buildings basically propped up by sandbags, more sandbags than masonry. As I was being led through very quickly by a guide called Elvira, I saw smoke coming up through the floor. I said, "Who's down there?" He said, "There are people living down there." I said, "Can we go and talk to them?" He said, "Don't be stupid, just quickly, you want to see this front-line and you want to get back." I looked through one of the sniper's holes in the sandbags. The front-line was the width of a street. There were bodies in the street and the Croats were literally on the other side. It is a front that line had held for nine months, and back to the other side; very frightening. We stayed in east Mostar on the night of 22nd February in the cellar and, in the meantime, out in the big wide real world, an American diplomat, Charles Redman, had been negotiating a peace between the Bosnian Army and the Croats, successfully. Word reached us in Mostar that day, the 22nd, that this peace was due for any minute now. I remember we were sitting in the cellar, "Can it hold? No, it cannot; it is impossible; how can it? It's ridiculous," said everybody. We thought we needed to get out and find out about this peace deal. So, we left. The next day, the day that the peace was due to come into effect -- and that is the 24th February -- we went into west Mostar. The first thing that I noticed was the contrast between west and east across the distance of a river. Petrol, cars, cafes open, soldiers chatting up the girls over coffee. Then the next thing one noticed was the extraordinary silence; there was no firing. Whatever treaty had been worked out in Washington and Zagreb had worked. We went to the HVO headquarters where we had to wait for, and speak to, a man called Veso Vegar who was the spokesman for the whole of the HVO in Bosnia. We asked him, "Is this really going to work? He said: "Yes, the cease-fire will be observed, the artillery is going to be redeployed in the case of" -- he used the term "recommencement" which I found interesting in itself -- "recommencement of hostilities with the Serbs". He reminded us that the HVO did not accept two armies in Mostar, but that the cease-fire and the agreement would be imposed and observed. We had some difficulty believing him and he said: "Come with me". He took a guard -- he did not actually come, he got a guard to drive us up to a mortar position. Quite apart from the fact that it was extraordinary to watch where we had been literally the morning before, under repeated shell fire, in the silence of a rather beautiful afternoon, was odd. The mortars were covered with caps -- leather caps. It was not that the crew were happy with it, one man said: "It is our town and I will take it apart rock by rock with my bear hands if I have to", but anyway the mortar was covered. The extraordinary thing was that that day this war, that began all the way back then in Novi Travnik, had ended. It was remarkable. We got back to Medzugorje and heard from colleagues that the same thing had happened in Vitez, Novi Travnik, all around the rest of Herzegovina, Tomislavgrad, all over, the whole thing had stopped; like turning a tap, flicking a switch. Even more quickly than it had been ignited, after the shot at the fuel station in Novi Travnik all that time ago, it had literally been turned off like a tap. The conclusion was unavoidable, a single chain of command, this machine worked, it worked well, it had work disastrously in October 1992, but efficiently, and it had worked -- thank God -- efficiently in February 1994, in ending the war. Barely a shot was fired since. One was then grateful for the coherence, cogency, and efficiency of that chain of command; it worked. I left Bosnia for a year in March 1994 and returned only some 10 months later to work on a retrospective series which backup a whole lot of other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the court's permission, if I can ask you some -- a very few follow-up questions concerning your testimony, Mr. Vulliamy. The first question I would like to direct you to is to the exhibit that is on the easel to your left. Mr. Dubuisson, that is Exhibit 29.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 29L.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using this particular blue marker and if I can ask -- with the assistance of the usher -- if we could take this off the easel. If you could mark the town of Prozor and mark out the road that you described as Route Diamond; could you do that for us, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you might have to pull it up on the easel a bit so you have something to lean on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked a lot --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, you have to put that microphone on if we could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I talked about Tomislavgrad. I am sorry, my back is to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue. Choose one or the other. Please continue, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the town of Prozor. (Indicating on map). (Inaudible due to witness microphone not functioning). Coming from Tomislavgrad, along here, there is Rumboci, which I mentioned. It becomes tarmac around here. Into Prozor and Route Diamond continues north from Prozor. It is a rough road here, but tarmac. Into Gornji Vakuf, turns off the main street of Gornji Vakuf, then becomes little more than a mountain track at this point, which improved during the war. Going north. (Indicating on map). Roughly like this, following these little communities, this old mountain track up into what is on this map called Pucarevo, which I have been calling by its new name, Novi Travnik. It comes out -- it comes out on the main road just to the north of Nova Bila there. Vitez is there. (Indicating on map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have marked that in blue on Exhibit 29L; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Route Diamond in blue, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could ask you, Mr. Vulliamy, to have a seat again and we will move to the next exhibit quickly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was intended to continue up north to Tuzla, but that is off this map and outside the scope of my direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not necessarily going in the chronology that you talked about, but we have a map of the Mostar area, which Mr. Dubuisson has before us. I believe that is Exhibit 306. (Handed). Now, Mr. Vulliamy, what you and I have done for clarification sake for the court is to mark some locations that you have discussed during your testimony; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the three cities or towns marked in orange down the centre. I believe those three represent the three camps that were controlled by the HVO that you discussed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They are in -- yes, they are in orange, Rodoc is the one south of Mostar, Dretelj just above Capljina and Gabela near the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that, in July of 1993, you had gone to the town of Capljina, that is designated just below Dretelj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Capljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you had met several individuals in -- Bosnian Muslim men in a camp in Dretelj from Stolac. That is marked on the right-hand side of the map, the lower right-hand corner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men said they came from there. I never went there myself. That is Stolac on the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, above Capljina and Dretelj was your main location in Medjugorje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Medjugorje here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked to us about a meeting in UNHCR -- that UNHCR discussed a conference on the Dalmatia Coast with the Republic of Croatian authorities and the Herceg-Bosna authorities, concerning the transfer of 50,000 Bosnian Muslim men to third countries; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that collection point supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The transit camp, as they called it, was supposed to be here in Ljubuski on the left of the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have that marked in green on the left of the map. We offer that as a frame of reference location, based on the testimony. If I can just address your attention to a couple of other matters you talked about. If I can turn my attention first to Exhibit 80/4. If we can put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which number is this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is 306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have that listed as 80/4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 80/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, naturally I am not asking you questions about everything you discussed, but you mentioned, in a conversation that you had with the BiH army commander, Kulenovic, and the HVO commander, Filip Filipovic, on top of Mount Vlasic in mid to late February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the individual that you were talking to Filip Filipovic, is he depicted in Photograph 80/6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is the man with the silver coloured hair there. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he sitting next to the defendant, Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted during your testimony that he said that he cursed Blaskic and Boban --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By name, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said that he was walking on the edge of a knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you conclude that he was concerned about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I concluded that he felt that he was being pushed; that these two men he named had made him walk the edge of a knife. By that, I took him to mean that he was being pushed by them to adhere to -- to obey orders that were, as I think he put it at another time, coming up the valley at him from Boban, from Vitez, to engage in a war against what he regarded as his Muslim allies, that he did not want to wage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to shift, once again, towards the end of your testimony. I want to show you, if you could, a document that has been received in evidence already as Exhibit 25, Mr. Dubuisson. This is an article, Mr. President, and your Honours, that has been previously submitted way back when, when Mr. Donia came into evidence. It is an article from Slobodan Dalmacija. The author of this article is an individual -- the by-line is given by the name of Veso Vegar. (Handed). Now, Mr. Vulliamy, you noted during the course of your testimony that, in the spring of 1993, after the Vance-Owen Plan was rejected by the Serbs, that there was a plan on behalf of the Bosnian Croats to implement their own plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I believe you mention that in your book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, I was following these events very closely from my neglected posts in London and in Italy, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not have this particular article published in Slobodan Dalmacija and authored by Veso Vegar, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you pick it up from a wire service article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I know, to the best of my recollection, Reuters reported this quite widely. They did not report the by-line or the origin of the paper, but they reported the point that it was making, which, as I said before, was that the HVO, now that the Vance-Owen Plan had been rejected by the Serbs, was going to unilaterally implement it -- or its understanding of it anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular article is written by Veso Vegar; is that the same Veso Vegar that you spoke to on February 23rd -- February 24th of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be amazed if I was wrong in presuming so, yes. Veso Vegar is the man that we had to see in west Mostar on the day that this war -- this bit of the war ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Veso Vegar a public information officer that a business would have or is this person an armed member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Veso Vegar was the spokesman for the HVO, and a powerful figure. No, he was not a PRO in a suit and tie. He was a man in military uniform and armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The individual that wrote this article on 4th April of 1993, in Slobodan Dalmacija, is the same individual that you see on February 23rd or 24th of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did events play out exactly as he said they were going to play out when he told you that the firing would stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely and mercifully so. He guaranteed the cease-fire would hold; it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy. Mr. President, and your Honours, I have no further questions of Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, now in order to organise our work -- I do not want to interrupt these proceedings in an untimely manner -- perhaps I might ask you how much time you think you would need, and please state quite frankly how much time you feel you need, or else we will have to ask the witness to come back next week or another time. The judges also obviously have questions they would wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would be surprised if I can conclude in less than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to know whether you needed another hour. Very well. I am sorry, sir, but would you be able to come back to appear here before this Tribunal on a date that will be decided later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it please the court, yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wanted to say that it is necessary. You do not have much choice on this matter. This is in order to clarify the proceedings. I did not want to interrupt the cross-examination. The Defence stated that he needs an hour, so even we had an entire afternoon, I was willing to go until 6.00 or 6.10, but I do not want for the colleagues and myself to have to be cut off as far as our questions are concerned. The judges, therefore, have decided to postpone the cross-examination and their own questions to a later date. There are, of course, transcripts, so we will have these to refresh our memories. I think this is much clearer. The witness has a great number of things to say. I do not want for the cross-examination, Mr. Hayman, to be forced. Therefore, I ask the Prosecution to try to find a later date that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before we conclude, I would remiss if I did not offer Exhibits 29L and 306 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have no objection. I would be remiss in not asking for a copy of the witness's notes from which he has read in conducting his testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a point of interest because what the witness was informed of was that if he made his own notes, that was not shown to either the Prosecutor or the Defence, that he would be able to keep his notes. That was a ruling, I believe, Mr. President, that your Honour made some time ago. Mr. Vulliamy has made his notes. He has not shown them to the Prosecutor. There is no need to give them over to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, the prior ruling of the court was that notes that were referred to from time to time were one thing. This is a statement that has been out. The court has seen the witness, the great detail, the dates, the constant reference to the notes. I think it is on the other side of the line. I will submit the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues on this issue because we all have our own practices in our own state systems. I come from a country which has its own criminal law system, in which a witness is interviewed or questioned without notes. But, of course, there are other systems that exist, so let me consult with my colleagues. (Pause). The Trial Chamber considers that these are private notes that need not be disclosed. The Chamber now stands adjourned. (5.25 pm)
